**Claim:** Yes. The set of equivalence classes of a.e.-equal bounded $\mathbb{R}$-valued functions on $\Omega$, equipped with $\|f\| = \operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|$, is a Banach space.

**Notation.** Let $X$ denote the set of bounded functions $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$, and let $\sim$ be the equivalence relation $f\sim g \iff f=g$ a.e. Write $[f]$ for the class of $f$ and $V = X/{\sim}$. Define $\|[f]\| := \operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|$. We must show (i) this is well-defined, (ii) it is a norm, and (iii) $V$ is complete.

---

### Step 1. Well-definedness on equivalence classes

Suppose $f\sim g$, so there is a null set $N$ with $f=g$ on $\Omega\setminus N$. For any null set $A$, set $A'=A\cup N$ (still null). Then
$$\sup_{x\notin A}|f(x)| \;\ge\; \sup_{x\notin A'}|f(x)| \;=\; \sup_{x\notin A'}|g(x)| \;\ge\; \operatorname{ess\,sup}|g|,$$
where the last inequality uses $A'$ as a competitor in the infimum defining $\operatorname{ess\,sup}|g|$. Taking $\inf$ over null $A$ gives $\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|\ge\operatorname{ess\,sup}|g|$. By symmetry, equality holds. ∎

### Step 2. Norm axioms

**Non-negativity and homogeneity** are immediate from the definition.

**Positive definiteness.** If $\|[f]\|=0$, then for every $n\ge1$ there is a null set $A_n$ with $|f(x)|<1/n$ for $x\notin A_n$. Set $A=\bigcup_n A_n$; this is null, and for $x\notin A$ we have $|f(x)|<1/n$ for all $n$, hence $f(x)=0$. So $f=0$ a.e., i.e., $[f]=0$.

**Triangle inequality.** Let $\varepsilon>0$. Choose null sets $A,B$ with $\sup_{x\notin A}|f(x)|<\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|+\varepsilon$ and $\sup_{x\notin B}|g(x)|<\operatorname{ess\,sup}|g|+\varepsilon$. Set $C=A\cup B$ (null). Then
$$\sup_{x\notin C}|f(x)+g(x)|\le\sup_{x\notin C}|f(x)|+\sup_{x\notin C}|g(x)|<\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|+\operatorname{ess\,sup}|g|+2\varepsilon.$$
Taking $\inf$ over null $C$ and then $\varepsilon\to0$:
$$\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f+g|\le\operatorname{ess\,sup}|f|+\operatorname{ess\,sup}|g|.\qquad\blacksquare$$

### Step 3. Completeness

Let $([f_n])_{n\ge1}$ be Cauchy in $V$. We construct a limit $[f]\in V$ with $\|f_n-f\|\to0$.

**Extract a fast subsequence.** Choose indices $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ with $\|f_{n_{k+1}}-f_{n_k}\|<2^{-k}$ for all $k\ge1$.

**Build null sets controlling the jumps.** For each $k$, pick a null set $A_k$ such that
$$|f_{n_{k+1}}(x)-f_{n_k}(x)|\le 2^{-k}\quad\text{for }x\notin A_k.$$
Set $A=\bigcup_{k\ge1}A_k$; this is null.

**Pointwise convergence off $A$.** For $x\notin A$ and $j>k$:
$$|f_{n_j}(x)-f_{n_k}(x)|\le\sum_{i=k}^{j-1}|f_{n_{i+1}}(x)-f_{n_i}(x)|\le\sum_{i=k}^{j-1}2^{-i}\le 2^{-k+1}.$$
So $(f_{n_k}(x))_{k\ge1}$ is Cauchy in $\mathbb{R}$, hence convergent. Define
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\lim_{k\to\infty}f_{n_k}(x),&x\notin A,\\[4pt] 0,&x\in A.\end{cases}$$

**$f$ is bounded.** Since $f_{n_1}$ is bounded, $|f_{n_1}(x)|\le M$ for all $x$. For $x\notin A$:
$$|f(x)|\le|f_{n_1}(x)|+\sum_{k\ge1}|f_{n_{k+1}}(x)-f_{n_k}(x)|\le M+\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}=M+1.$$
For $x\in A$, $f(x)=0$. Thus $f$ is bounded, so $[f]\in V$.

**The subsequence converges to $f$.** For $x\notin A$ and $j>k$ we showed $|f_{n_j}(x)-f_{n_k}(x)|\le 2^{-k+1}$; letting $j\to\infty$:
$$|f(x)-f_{n_k}(x)|\le 2^{-k+1}\quad\text{for }x\notin A.$$
Since $A$ is null, $\|f-f_{n_k}\|\le 2^{-k+1}\to0$.

**The full sequence converges to $f$.** Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $(f_n)$ is Cauchy, there exists $N$ with $\|f_m-f_n\|<\varepsilon$ for $m,n\ge N$. Choose $k$ large enough that $n_k\ge N$ and $2^{-k+1}<\varepsilon$. Then for any $n\ge N$:
$$\|f_n-f\|\le\|f_n-f_{n_k}\|+\|f_{n_k}-f\|<\varepsilon+2^{-k+1}<2\varepsilon.$$
Hence $\|f_n-f\|\to0$.

---

### Conclusion

$(V,\|\cdot\|)$ is a normed vector space (Steps 1–2) in which every Cauchy sequence converges (Step 3). Therefore it is a **Banach space**. $\blacksquare$
